# The cards

87 cards, every one a batch table can name in its `workflow` column. For each: its id (what
goes in the cell), the title students see, the model it runs, what it does in plain words, the
technical description, and the columns a row gives it. The `id`, `workflow`, `repeat` and `notes`
columns work on every card. Inputs take a row id, `file:`, `folder:`, `job:` or `empty`: see
[../SKILL.md](../SKILL.md) and [docs/batch-format.md](../../docs/batch-format.md).

A storyboard (.md) uses only the six cards named in [workflows.md](workflows.md).

## 3D (`3d`, 6)

### `3d_mesh_uv_unwrap`

**Prepare a 3D model for texturing** · model: **UV unwrap & bake AO - prepare a model for texturing** · makes **model3d** · experimental

Give it a 3D model and get the same model back ready for painting or texturing, with an image of how its surface was flattened and a map of its soft shadows.

> Upload a 3D model (GLB, GLTF, OBJ or STL - convert a PLY or FBX file to GLB first) and get back the same model with a clean UV layout, plus the two maps that layout makes possible. This is what lets you paint or bake textures onto a mesh that arrived without usable UVs - which most generated and scanned meshes do. It cuts the surface into islands, packs them into one square atlas, and bakes an ambient-occlusion map from the ORIGINAL geometry: the soft contact shadows in creases and crevices that make a model read as solid rather than flat. RESULTS: the .glb carrying the new UVs, a UV layout PNG (each island in its own colour, so you can see how the surface was cut and packed), and the AO map PNG. Atlas resolution drives all three stages at once - the unwrap, the layout render and the AO bake. Rays per texel trades AO quality against time. Island splitting: 'pec' is the general-purpose cut, 'adaptive' sizes islands by how much detail the surface carries there. Time scales with how dense the model is, not with the atlas size: about 15 s for a few thousand triangles, about 45 s for half a million. Unlike the remesh bundle this one is not fussy about the model's scale - it was checked on the same mesh at 50x difference and produced the same atlas and the same AO.

Columns: `model3d` 3D model (GLB, GLTF, OBJ or STL) (model3d, required)

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):
  - `primitiveint_value_2` Atlas resolution (px) — 256…4096, step 256; default 2048
  - `unwrapmesh_segmenter_8` Island splitting — one of: pec, adaptive; default pec
  - `primitiveint_value_3` Padding between islands (px) — 0…16, step 1; default 1
  - `primitiveint_value_4` AO rays per texel — 4…1024, step 4; default 64
  - `primitivefloat_value_5` AO strength — 0…2, step 0.05; default 1

### `3d_mesh_remesh_decimate`

**Turn a 3D model low-poly** · model: **Remesh & decimate - 3D model to clean low-poly** · makes **model3d** · experimental

Give it a heavy 3D model and get back a clean, closed, lightweight version at the triangle count you choose, ready for games, the web or 3D printing.

> Upload a 3D model (GLB, GLTF, OBJ or STL - convert a PLY or FBX file to GLB first) and get back a clean, low-poly version at the triangle count you ask for. This is the step between a generated or scanned mesh and something you can actually use in a game engine, a real-time viewer or a 3D print. WATERTIGHT REMESH (on by default) rebuilds the surface from scratch as one closed shell. It removes holes, duplicate faces and interior junk, and it lets the decimator land almost exactly on your target. Turn it OFF to keep the original surface and merely weld and simplify it; it is the fallback when the remesh comes back empty. Either way the result has no UVs: run 'Prepare a 3D model for texturing' (UV unwrap & bake AO) afterwards if you need them. WHEN IT COMES BACK EMPTY - measured on this rig, not guessed: the watertight remesh only works on a model at a sane scale, roughly a few units across. A mesh exported in millimetres (hundreds of units across) comes back EMPTY, with no error and no 3D file. Two of nine test meshes failed this way, the Stanford Bunny among them, and the same mesh scaled down 50x then worked. The giveaway is the second stat panel reading 'Faces: 0'. Fix it by turning Watertight remesh off, or by rescaling the model before you upload it. RESULTS: the remeshed .glb, plus two text panels - your model's vertex and face count BEFORE, then the result's AFTER, so you can see exactly what the reduction cost you.

Columns: `model3d` 3D model (GLB, GLTF, OBJ or STL) (model3d, required)

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):
  - `primitiveint_value_2` Target triangle count — 100…500000, step 100; default 2000
  - `primitiveboolean_value_3` Watertight remesh (rebuild as one closed shell) — yes / no; default true
  - `primitiveint_value_4` Smoothing passes (watertight remesh only) — 0…20, step 1; default 2
  - `primitivefloat_value_5` Sharp-edge angle (degrees, 180 = fully smooth) — 0…180, step 1; default 90

### `3d_triposplat_image_to_gaussian_splat`

**Turn a picture into 3D, fast** · model: **TripoSplat — image to 3D** · makes **model3d**

Give it one picture of an object and get a soft 3D 'splat' in seconds, plus a rough mesh. Great for fluffy, leafy or stylised things; less good for people.

> Upload a single image of an object and get back a 3D Gaussian splat plus an extracted polygon mesh. Use a clean, well-lit photo with the subject centered. Leave 'Auto-remove background' on for photos with a busy background; turn it off only for a PNG whose background is already transparent (a plain white or grey backdrop is kept as part of the 3D object). 'Number of gaussians' runs from 32,768 to 1,048,576; above 262,144 the splat gets denser but gains no new detail. Outputs: a Gaussian splat (.spz) you can spin in the splat viewer, a .ply splat export, and a .glb mesh.

Columns: `seed` · `image` Source image (image, required)

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):
  - `switch_mask_source_88_35` Auto-remove background — yes / no; default true
  - `ksampler_steps_88_6` Steps — 1…60, step 1; default 20
  - `vaedecodetriposplat_num_gaussians_88_55` Number of gaussians — 32768…1048576, step 32768; default 1048576

### `3d_idol_image_to_gaussian_splat`

**Turn a picture into 3D, with a turntable video** · model: **IDOL — image to 3D** · makes **video**

Give it one picture of an object or a character and get a soft 3D "splat", a rough mesh and a short video that turns around it. A sibling of TripoSplat, with its own model.

> IDOL, run through ComfyUI's TripoSplat nodes: one picture in, a 3D Gaussian splat out. Use a clean picture with the subject in the middle. Leave "Remove the background" on for a photo with a busy background; turn it off only for a PNG whose background is already transparent. Outputs: the splat (.spz) to spin in the splat viewer, a mesh (.glb) extracted from it, and a 3-second video orbiting the splat.

Columns: `seed` · `image` Picture of the object (image, required)

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):
  - `switch_mask_source_88_35` Remove the background — yes / no; default true
  - `ksampler_steps_88_6` Steps — 4…50, step 1; default 20
  - `vaedecodetriposplat_num_gaussians_88_55` Number of gaussians — 32768…1048576, step 32768; default 262144

### `3d_pixal3d_trellis2_image_to_model`

**Turn a picture into textured 3D** · model: **Pixal3D / TRELLIS.2 (built-in nodes) — image to PBR-textured 3D model** · makes **model3d**

Give it one clear picture of an object or character and get a detailed 3D model with colour and material maps that you can spin, download and use.

> Upload one image of an object or character and get back a 3D model (.glb) with full PBR materials — colour, metallic, roughness, normal and ambient-occlusion maps baked in — that you can spin in the viewer. This version runs entirely on ComfyUI's own built-in 3D nodes and can use two different generators: Pixal3D (the default) also estimates the camera of your picture so the shape lines up closely with what you see, while TRELLIS.2 (tick 'Use TRELLIS.2') is an alternative worth trying when Pixal3D struggles with a subject. Use a clean, well-lit picture with the whole subject visible. Leave 'Auto-remove background' on for normal photos; turn it off only for a PNG that already has a transparent background. 'Shape detail' sets how finely the geometry is sampled (higher = more detail, more memory and time). 'Target face count' is the polygon budget of the final mesh — lower is lighter to view and share. 'Texture resolution' sets the colour, metallic and roughness maps (4096 is crisp, 2048 gives a much smaller file); the normal map is always baked at 2048 and the ambient-occlusion map at 1024. Generation, remeshing, UV unwrapping and texture baking all run in one go, so expect a few minutes per model.

Columns: `seed` · `image` Object image (whole subject in frame) (image, required)

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):
  - `primitiveboolean_value_316` Use TRELLIS.2 instead of Pixal3D — yes / no; default false
  - `comfyswitchnode_switch_248` Auto-remove background (turn off only for a transparent PNG) — yes / no; default true
  - `trellis2upsamplestage_target_resolution_94` Shape detail (voxel resolution — higher = finer, more memory & time) — 1024…2048, step 128; default 1536
  - `decimatemesh_target_face_count_186` Target face count (polygon budget of the final mesh) — 10000…2000000, step 10000; default 700000
  - `primitiveint_value_288` Texture resolution (colour, metallic and roughness maps) — 1024…8192, step 1024; default 4096

### `3d_pixal3d_multi_views`

**Turn four views into 3D** · model: **Pixal3D Multi-View — 4 views to PBR-textured 3D model** · makes **model3d**

Give it four pictures of the same thing (front, both sides and back) and get one 3D model with materials. Pick it when the back and sides must be right, not guessed.

> Upload four pictures of the same character or object — front, left side, back and right side — and Pixal3D rebuilds it as one 3D model (.glb) with PBR materials (colour, metallic, roughness, normal and ambient-occlusion maps) that you can spin in the viewer. Because the model sees the subject from every side, the back and sides come out far more faithfully than from a single picture. The four views should look like a turnaround sheet: the same subject at the same size, straight-on views (as flat and orthographic as possible), on a plain background. Renders and AI-generated turnaround views work best; casual phone photos much less so. If you have one sheet with all four poses side by side, cut it into four separate images first. The background is removed and each view is framed automatically. 'Shape detail' sets how finely the geometry is sampled (higher = more detail, more memory and time). 'Target face count' is the polygon budget of the final mesh — lower is lighter to view and share. 'Texture resolution' sets the colour, metallic and roughness maps (4096 is crisp, 2048 gives a much smaller file); the normal map is always baked at 2048 and the ambient-occlusion map at 1024. Expect a few minutes per model.

Columns: `seed` · `image` Front view (image, required) · `image2` Left side view (image, required) · `image3` Back view (image, required) · `image4` Right side view (image, required)

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):
  - `trellis2upsamplestage_target_resolution_94` Shape detail (voxel resolution — higher = finer, more memory & time) — 1024…2048, step 128; default 1536
  - `decimatemesh_target_face_count_186` Target face count (polygon budget of the final mesh) — 10000…2000000, step 10000; default 700000
  - `primitiveint_value_288` Texture resolution (colour, metallic and roughness maps) — 1024…8192, step 1024; default 4096

## Sound and music (`audio`, 2)

### `audio_yue2_music_cover`

**Cover a song in another style** · model: **YuE2 music cover - re-sing a song in a new style** · makes **audio** · experimental

Give it a song plus new words or a new style, and it sings the same tune again as a completely different performance.

> Upload a song and get back a cover of it: YuE2 lifts the melody out of your recording as a score, then performs it again as a new piece of music, in whatever style you describe and with whatever lyrics you write. It is a COVER tool, not a remix - nothing of the original recording survives into the result. What carries over is the tune. So a piano ballad can come back as a brass-band stomp, and it will still be recognisably the same song. STYLE is the production brief, not a genre word: language, genre, the voice you want, the tempo, and the instruments, e.g. 'English, soulful jazz-pop, expressive male vocal, relaxed 88 BPM, Rhodes piano, upright bass, brushed drums'. The more concrete the instrument list, the closer the arrangement lands. LYRICS are sung as written, and the section tags matter: mark them [Verse], [Chorus], [Bridge] so the model knows where the song lifts. WHAT TO FOLLOW: 'melody' takes the tune alone and is the recommended setting for covers; 'full' takes the melody and the chords too, which holds the harmony closer but leaves the arrangement less room to change. The one control sets it for both the transcription and the generation, which have to agree - if they disagree the score is read against the wrong expectation. LENGTH follows the LYRICS and the extracted score, not the length of the song you uploaded - a 20-second reference with three verses of lyrics produced 98 seconds of music. 'Maximum length' is the ceiling, not the target. Result: one audio file (FLAC). Licence: YuE2 is a research model - check its terms before any commercial use, and only upload music you have the right to work from.

Prompting: [YuE - writing covers (style & lyrics)](https://github.com/multimodal-art-projection/YuE/blob/main/docs/covers.md) · [YuE2 - generation and covers reference](https://github.com/multimodal-art-projection/YuE/blob/main/skills/yue2-music/references/generation-and-covers.md)
Tip: Style is a production brief: language, genre, voice, tempo, instruments. Tag lyric sections [Verse] / [Chorus] / [Bridge].

Columns: `prompt` (Style - language, genre, voice, tempo, instruments) · `seed` · `audio` Reference song (the tune to cover) (audio, required)

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):
  - `yue2generatemusic_lyrics_33_25` Lyrics (tag sections [Verse] / [Chorus] / [Bridge]); default [Verse] Streetlights shimmer on the pavement Midnight breat…
  - `sheetsage2audiotoabc_mode_33_41` What to follow from the song — one of: melody, full; default melody
  - `yue2generatemusic_max_duration_33_25` Maximum length (seconds) — 10…900, step 1; default 360
  - `yue2generatemusic_temperature_33_25` Temperature (higher = more adventurous) — 0…5, step 0.05; default 1

### `audio_stable_audio_3_medium`

**Make music or sound effects** · model: **Stable Audio 3 Medium — text to audio** · makes **audio**

Describe the music, loop or sound effect you want and get it in seconds, up to five minutes long. Instrumental only: it does not sing.

> Generate music, instrument loops, sound effects, or one-shots from a short text description. Type what you want (e.g. "lofi hip-hop chill beat with mellow Rhodes and vinyl crackle"), set a duration, and play the result. 'Enhance prompt with AI' is off by default; switched on, a small Qwen 3.5 model rewrites your description first (about 15 seconds). Or write the full description yourself, the way Stability's guide recommends: genre first, then instruments, mood, production and tempo (BPM) — or a plain description of one sound effect. The Category menu only steers that AI rewrite, so it has no effect while the enhancer is off. It does not sing.

Prompting: [Stable Audio 3 prompt guide (Stability AI)](https://stability.ai/guides/stable-audio-3-prompt-guide)
Tip: Genre first, then instruments, mood, production and tempo (BPM) — or describe one sound effect plainly. It does not sing.

Columns: `prompt` (Description) · `seed`

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):
  - `category_52_43` Category — one of: Music, Instrument, SFX, One-shot; default Music
  - `enhance_prompt_52_35` Enhance prompt with AI (a small Qwen 3.5 model rewrites your description first; adds about 15 seconds) — yes / no; default false
  - `duration_seconds_52_36` Duration (seconds) — 1…300, step 1; default 150
  - `steps_52_3` Steps — 1…50, step 1; default 8

## Describing a picture or a video in words (`description`, 2)

### `describe_gemma4_image_description`

**Describe a picture in words** · model: **Gemma 4 — describe an image (caption)** · makes **text**

Give it a picture and it writes about it: a description, the exact text it can read, or a prompt to make a similar picture.

> Ask Gemma 4 (a vision-language model running in ComfyUI) to describe an image in words. Upload an image and the model writes a caption / description as text — useful on its own, or to turn a picture into a prompt for another workflow. Edit the instruction to steer the output, e.g. "Describe the image," / "List the main objects." / "Write a short caption." / "Describe the mood and lighting." Change the seed to re-roll the wording.

Prompting: [Gemma — understanding pictures (Google)](https://ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/capabilities/vision)
Tip: Ask for exactly what you want back: a description, the text it can read, a list, or a prompt to make a similar picture.

Columns: `prompt` (Instruction) · `seed` · `image` Source image (image, required)

### `describe_gemma4_video_description`

**Describe a video in words** · model: **Gemma 4 — describe a video (caption)** · makes **text**

Give it a short video and it writes what happens, second by second. It looks at one frame in every 24 and does not hear the sound, so its times are true seconds only for a 24 fps clip.

> Ask Gemma 4 (a vision-language model running in ComfyUI) to describe a video in words. Upload a clip and the model writes a description / caption as text — useful on its own, or to turn a video into a prompt for another workflow. Edit the instruction to steer the output, e.g. "Describe the video." / "List what happens, step by step." / "Write a short caption." / "Describe the mood, motion and lighting." Change the seed to re-roll the wording. Tip: keep clips short. The whole clip is decoded first, then the model looks at one frame in every 24 (one a second for a 24 fps clip), each shrunk small, and it does not hear the sound. So very long or 4K clips take longer and use more memory, and quick events between those frames can be missed. The times it writes (00:01, 00:02…) count those frames, so they are real seconds only for a 24 fps clip: on a 30 fps phone clip, "00:10" is really about 8 seconds in.

Prompting: [Gemma — understanding video (Google)](https://ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/capabilities/vision/video)

Columns: `prompt` (Instruction) · `seed` · `video` Source video (video, required)

## Picture to picture (enlarging, restoring) (`i2i`, 4)

### `utility_pid_image_upscale`

**Make a picture poster-sized, 4× bigger** · model: **PiD — image upscale ×4 (up to 33 MP)** · makes **image**

Give it a clean, sharp picture and get it back 4 times wider and taller (up to 33 megapixels) with the same colours and content. Pick it for printing or zooming in, not for damaged photos.

> Upload an image and NVIDIA's PiD pixel decoder rebuilds it 4× wider and 4× taller: a 1920×1080 picture becomes 7680×4320 (33 MP), a 1024×1024 one becomes 4096×4096. Each side is first trimmed to a multiple of 8 pixels (at most 7 pixels, shared between opposite edges), so the result is exactly 4× of that: a 1234×567 picture comes back 4928×2240. It adds real fine detail (fabric, foliage, stone, skin) instead of just enlarging the pixels, and keeps the original colours. The image is processed in overlapping tiles, so there are no visible seams. Big photos are first shrunk to fit 1920×1080 by the upload form, so the largest result is 7680×4320. Clean, sharp images give the best results. Tiny, blurry or heavily compressed pictures (for example ones saved from a messaging app) can come back with invented texture or odd-looking small faces. The result files are very large (tens of MB), so opening and downloading them takes a moment. Change the seed to re-roll the fine detail.

Columns: `seed` · `image` Image to upscale (image, required)

### `utility_seedvr2_4k_upscale`

**Rebuild a photo's detail at 4K** · model: **SeedVR2 — image upscale to 4K** · makes **image**

Give it a photo, even a noisy or slightly blurry one, and get it back up to 4K with real detail rebuilt: fur, skin, fabric, foliage. The most detailed of the photo enlargers.

> Upscale and restore a picture with SeedVR2, a diffusion super-resolution model that rebuilds real detail - skin, hair, fabric, grain - rather than just sharpening what is already there. It is the closest thing on this machine to a "creative" upscaler. How the output size is worked out, because it surprises people. The first setting is the target for the SHORTEST edge, and the aspect ratio is always preserved exactly. The second is a hard cap on the LONGEST edge, and it wins: if the two disagree, the picture comes out smaller than you asked. Worked example on a wide 1234x567 photograph. Ask for 2048 with the cap at 4096 and the long edge would be 4457, over the cap, so you get 4096x1882 - and asking for 4096 instead gives the very same picture, because the cap decides. Raise the cap to 8192 and you get the 4456x2048 you actually asked for. So on anything far from square, set the cap first. Odd sizes are fine. Any width and height work, including numbers that are not round or divisible by 8, and the aspect ratio is kept to within a pixel of rounding. It is a heavy model and a slow run, more so at high settings. If the invented detail looks wrong, change the seed and run it again - the model makes up plausible texture, so a different seed makes up different texture.

Columns: `seed` · `image` Source image (image, required)

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):
  - `resolution_10` Detail level - target size of the SHORTEST edge in pixels — 512…4096, step 64; default 4096
  - `max_resolution_10` Cap on the LONGEST edge - raise it for wide or tall pictures, or the setting above is ignored — 1024…8192, step 256; default 4096

### `utility_seedvr2_7b_int8_image_upscale`

**Rebuild a photo's detail, fast** · model: **SeedVR2 7B (int8) — image upscale & restore (up to 4K)** · makes **image**

Give it a photo and get it back up to 4 times bigger with lost detail rebuilt. About twice as fast as the 4K version, and it can match the original colours.

> Upload a photo or render and SeedVR2 rebuilds it up to 4× larger, adding realistic detail (skin, hair, fabric, foliage) rather than just sharpening. This is the int8 build of the 7B model, running on ComfyUI's built-in SeedVR2 support. Your image is first shrunk so its longest side is at most 1024 px, then multiplied by the upscale factor — ×4 gives about 4K (4096 px on the long side). Lower factors are faster. If the colours shift compared with the original, pick a colour correction ("lab" is the most faithful). Change the seed to re-roll the generated detail.

Columns: `seed` · `image` Image to upscale (image, required)

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):
  - `resizeimagemasknode_resize_type_multiplier_66_57` Upscale factor (×4 ≈ 4K from a 1024 px image) — 1…4, step 0.5; default 4
  - `seedvr2postprocessing_color_correction_method_66_59` Colour correction (match the original colours) — one of: lab, wavelet, adain, none; default none

### `utility_qwen_2511_unblur_upscale`

**Sharpen a blurry portrait** · model: **Unblur & upscale a photo (Qwen Image Edit 2511)** · makes **image**

Give it a small or blurry photo of a person and get a sharper version (about 1 megapixel) that keeps the same face. Pick it for portraits; use the other enlargers for everything else.

> Sharpen a blurry or low-resolution photograph. Upload a picture and the model re-renders it, recovering detail — it was trained above all to bring back FACES in partly blurred pictures. Read this before judging it. The adapter's own author says plainly: "This adapter was experimental and trained to recover facial patterns from partially blurred images. The base model produces better overall quality, but it does not preserve those patterns." So it is a trade, not a straight improvement — the adapter holds on to a face's identity, while the model without it may give you a cleaner picture of someone slightly different. Set "Adapter strength" to 0 to see the base model on the same picture and judge for yourself. This is a RE-RENDER, not an enlarger. The picture comes back at roughly 1 megapixel whatever you put in, so it genuinely enlarges a small or soft picture but will not turn a photo into a poster. For pure enlargement use the PiD upscaler (exactly 4x) or the SeedVR2 upscalers instead. Because it re-renders, it can also invent: a face can come back subtly changed, and small print or logos can turn to nonsense. Check the result against your original before using it for anything that matters. Four training checkpoints are installed. The author recommends 20 or 15; 5 and 10 are there so you can see how the effect builds up. Licence: Apache 2.0 for the adapter — unusually permissive for this family. The Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 base model it runs on is Apache 2.0 as well (its Hugging Face card).

Prompting: [Qwen-Image-Edit-2511-Unblur-Upscale - the adapter](https://huggingface.co/prithivMLmods/Qwen-Image-Edit-2511-Unblur-Upscale)
Tip: The trigger phrase "unblur and upscale" is added for you. The author recommends checkpoint 20 or 15, and warns the base model alone gives better overall quality but loses facial identity.

Columns: `seed` · `image` The blurry or low-resolution picture (image, required)

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):
  - `textencodeqwenimageeditplus_prompt_427_221_151` Anything to add (optional; the trigger words "unblur and upscale" are added for you)
  - `loraloadermodelonly_lora_name_427_221_220` Training checkpoint (20 and 15 are the author's picks); default Qwen-Image-Edit-Unblur-Upscale_20.safetensors
  - `loraloadermodelonly_strength_model_427_221_220` Adapter strength - set to 0 to see the base model on the same picture — 0…1.5, step 0.05; default 1
  - `primitiveboolean_value_427_221_168` Fast mode (4 steps instead of 40 - leave on unless the result looks thin) — yes / no; default true

## Making a video (`i2v`, 18)

### `video_pika_h3_flex_fl2va`

**Animate between two pictures, polished** · model: **Pika H3 Flex — first / last frame to video with sound (6 steps)** · makes **video** · experimental

Give a first picture and, if you like, a last one, and describe what happens in between; you get a large, smooth video with sound that starts on the first and ends exactly on the second.

> A picture becomes the opening shot of a video WITH sound — and optionally a second picture becomes where it ends. Six sampling steps (Pika H3 Flex on MiniMax H3). The video takes the shape of the first picture. Describe how it moves from the first frame to the last: what happens and when ("at about two seconds…"), the camera move, and the sound. It generates the soundtrack with the picture — say what is heard (dialogue in quotes, effects, ambience, music) or you get whatever it invents. With a last picture, say in the prompt that the shot ends on it. Leave it empty for a plain image-to-video. Durations from 5 to 15 seconds.

Prompting: [Pika H3 Flex — prompt guide](https://github.com/Pika-Labs/Pika-H3-Flex/blob/main/docs/prompt-guidance.md) · [MiniMax H3 — official prompt guide](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3/blob/main/docs/VIDEO_PROMPT_WRITING_GUIDE_base_en.md) · [Pika H3 Flex — model card and showcase prompts](https://huggingface.co/Pika-Labs/Pika-H3-Flex)
Tip: Say what is in frame and what must stay the same, then the shots: start with [Shot 1] (no time), give each later shot one cut time ([Shot 2] At 00:02.000, …) rather than a range, and describe the camera moves in words; then the sound and the music. Ask for real-time motion if you do not want slow motion.

Columns: `prompt` (Prompt — from the first frame to the last, and the sound) · `seed` · `image` First frame — the video starts on this picture and takes its shape (image, required) · `image2` Last frame — optional, the video ends on it (image, optional)

### `video_fastvideo_fasth3_t2v`

**Draft a longer video with sound** · model: **FastVideo FastH3 — text to video with sound (8 steps)** · makes **video**

Another fast text-to-video engine, best for calm, cinematic scenes of up to 12 seconds with several shots, a narrator and music. For short, lively clips the quick video card, "Make a quick video with sound" (MiniMax H3, 4-step turbo), is faster on this machine.

> Write a scene and get a short film back WITH its soundtrack — dialogue, effects and music are generated together with the picture, in sync. This is MiniMax H3 distilled to 8 sampling steps by FastVideo, so it is several times quicker than the full model for a small loss of detail. Describe it like a shot list: camera angle and movement, what is in frame, what happens, and then the sound. The model was trained on descriptions that name the audio explicitly — "we hear footsteps on gravel and distant traffic" earns you that soundtrack; saying nothing about sound gets you whatever it invents. Duration is in seconds at 24 fps and is snapped to the model’s own frame grid. Keep clips short: cost grows with length and with resolution. The default is 0.9 megapixels (1280x736 in 16:9): a 5-second clip takes about 2 minutes once the models are loaded, and a 10-second one took 5.5 minutes. At 0.4 megapixels (864x480), the size of ComfyUI's template, it is two to three times faster but the fur, leaves and textures come out soft and smeared: use it only for a quick draft of the motion. Text to video. The same 8-step checkpoint can also start or end on a picture — that is the "Start or end on your picture" card (FastVideo FastH3 — first and/or last frame). For short, lively clips the 4-step MiniMax H3 turbo card is faster on this machine; this one suits calm, cinematic scenes with several shots.

Prompting: [MiniMax H3 — official video prompt guide](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3/blob/main/docs/VIDEO_PROMPT_WRITING_GUIDE_base_en.md) · [FastVideo FastH3 8-Step V2 — the distilled checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/FastVideo/FastVideo-FastH3-8-Step-V2)
Tip: Write shot by shot: framing and camera move, subject and action, setting and light — then say what is heard. Naming the audio is what gets you a deliberate soundtrack.

The timeline books the time of the default size, so a 2K job runs past its slot. Length is fixed at 124 frames (about 5 s at 24 fps). Needs the node pack **ComfyUI-Open-H3-Regenerate-2K** (1038lab, GPL-3.0) for the one refine node; everything else is core ComfyUI. Sharp curve is off: its 50 curve branches are all zero, so it adds nothing.

Give a first and a last picture and describe what happens in between; it makes the video that travels from one to the other, with sound. Pick it when a shot must end exactly on a picture you chose.

> Give a START image and an END image and LTX 2.5 generates a short video that travels from the first frame to the last, with a matching audio track. In the prompt, describe what happens in between — the motion, the camera move, and the sounds (e.g. "The hand slowly opens and a glowing crystal appears above the palm; a low hum rises"). Both images are resized and center-cropped to the width × height you choose (1280×704 by default; sizes move in steps of 64 pixels), so use two pictures with the same framing and aspect ratio. Resolution, duration and frame rate drive the generation time far more than anything else. "Enhance prompt with AI" (off by default) lets a small built-in language model look at the first frame and expand a short prompt into a detailed cinematic one — useful for one-line prompts, but it adds a minute or two.

Prompting: [LTX prompting guide — Lightricks](https://docs.ltx.io/open-source-model/usage-guides/prompting-guide) · [LTX-2.5 prompt guide — Lightricks blog](https://ltx.io/blog/ltx-2-5-prompt-guide)
Tip: One flowing paragraph in the present tense (4–8 sentences) about what happens: the action in order, the camera movement and the sound, with spoken lines in "quotes". Don't re-describe what is already visible in the image.

Columns: `prompt` (Prompt (motion + sound)) · `seed` · `image` First frame (image, required) · `image2` Last frame (image, required)

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):
  - `primitiveboolean_value_251_250` Enhance prompt with AI (slower) — yes / no; default false
  - `primitiveint_value_251_215` Width (px, multiple of 64) — 256…1920, step 64; default 1280
  - `primitiveint_value_251_216` Height (px, multiple of 64) — 256…1920, step 64; default 704
  - `primitiveint_value_251_198` Duration (seconds) — 1…10, step 1; default 5
  - `primitiveint_value_251_205` Frame rate (fps) — 8…30, step 1; default 24

### `video_minimax_h3_seamless_loop`

**Make a video that loops forever** · model: **MiniMax H3 — seamless looping video with sound** · makes **video** · experimental

Describe something that keeps going — breathing, swaying, spinning — and get a clip with sound whose end flows straight back into its start, so it can play endlessly. Takes several minutes.

> A video with its own soundtrack whose last frame flows straight back into its first, so it can play forever. No first/last frame, no crossfade: the pack makes the model join the end of the clip to its start while it samples, then smooths the whole loop with frame interpolation (the joint included). Whether the joint is invisible depends mostly on the PROMPT. Describe a state that keeps going, not events: a locked-off camera ("Locked-off static camera, no pan, no zoom."), one large subject doing one cyclic thing (pulsing, rotating, swaying, drifting), steady light, and a steady overall_soundscape. Avoid timelines, "then" and "finally", one-off events (a bite, a blink) and anything that piles up (spills, footprints) — it resets at the joint. A reference picture is optional: upload one and call it <Picture 1> in the prompt to hold the subject and look. Fast mode uses the 8-step turbo LoRA v1.1; turn it off for 25 steps, which the author finds smoothest on fast motion (about 3× slower). The seed decides a lot — try several before blaming the prompt. Expect several minutes per loop.

Prompting: [MiniMax H3 Loop — prompting guide](https://github.com/pxl-pshr/ComfyUI-MiniMaxH3-Loop/blob/main/PROMPTING.md) · [MiniMax H3 Loop — the node pack](https://github.com/pxl-pshr/ComfyUI-MiniMaxH3-Loop)
Tip: Describe a state that keeps going, not a sequence of events: locked-off camera, one subject doing one cyclic thing, steady light and sound. Ask: if this played twice in a row, would the joint show?

Columns: `prompt` (Prompt — a state that keeps going, not a sequence of events) · `seed` · `image` Reference picture (optional) — call it <Picture 1> in the prompt (image, optional)

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):
  - `fast_mode_50` Fast mode — turbo LoRA, 8 steps (about 3× faster; off = 25 steps, smoothest on fast motion) — yes / no; default true
  - `length_9` Loop length in frames (107 = 4.25 s, 158 = 6.4 s, 209 = 8.5 s, 260 = 10.6 s, 311 = 12.75 s) — longer takes pr… — one of: 107, 158, 209, 260, 311; default 107
  - `width_9` Width (px) — 512…1344, step 32; default 1024
  - `height_9` Height (px) — 512…1344, step 32; default 576
  - `views_3` Clean sound at the loop point: 2 = on (about 1.8× slower), 1 = off (the sound can garble at the joint) — one of: 2, 1; default 2
  - `multiplier_23` Smoothing — frame interpolation across the whole loop: 2 = 48 fps, 3 = 72 fps, 4 = 96 fps — one of: 2, 3, 4; default 2

### `video_fastvideo_fasth3_omniref_r2v`

**Put your pictures in a video** · model: **FastVideo FastH3 OmniRef — video with sound from reference pictures (8 steps)** · makes **video** · experimental

Upload up to four pictures — a character, an object, a place — and write the scene; they appear together in a new 5-second film with voices and sound. The fast version.

> Give it up to four pictures — a character, a product, a place — and get a short film with its own soundtrack in which they appear. The model reuses what is in the pictures and invents the performance, the camera and the sound. Pictures are numbered in the order of the upload slots, so fill them from the top: the second slot is <Picture 2>, and so on. An empty slot is removed from the graph. Write the prompt in the model's sections, as in the default: **subject_definitions** ("<Subject 1> is the plane in <Picture 1>: …"), a one-line **summary**, **retention_analysis** (what must stay the same), **detailed_description** with one line per [Shot] and its timestamp, then **overall_soundscape** and **non_diegetic_music**. Naming the sounds is what gets a deliberate soundtrack. This is FastVideo's FastH3 OmniRef, MiniMax H3 distilled to 8 steps for reference-to-video. Plain text-to-video works but is not its strength — use the FastH3 text-to-video card for that.

Prompting: [MiniMax H3 — reference-video prompt guide](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3/blob/main/docs/VIDEO_PROMPT_WRITING_GUIDE_ref_en.md) · [FastH3 OmniRef — the distilled checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/FastVideo/FastH3-Omni-Comfy)
Tip: Define each <Subject N> from its <Picture N>, say what must be preserved, then write one line per [Shot] with its timestamp, and describe the sound.

Columns: `prompt` (Prompt — define the subjects from <Picture N>, then the shots and the sound) · `seed` · `image` Picture 1 — a character, product or place to reuse (image, required) · `image2` Picture 2 — optional (image, optional) · `image3` Picture 3 — optional (image, optional) · `image4` Picture 4 — optional (image, optional)

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):
  - `aspect_ratio_115` Shape of the video — one of: 1:1 (Square), 2:3 (Portrait Photo), 3:2 (Photo), 3:4 (Portrait Standard), 4:3 (Standard), 9:16 (Portrait Widescreen), 16:9 (Widescreen), 21:9 (Ultrawide); default 16:9 (Widescreen)
  - `megapixels_115` Size in megapixels (at 16:9: 0.4 ≈ 864×480, 1.0 ≈ 1376×768; the model was trained at 1344×768, about 0.98 MP) — 0.2…1, step 0.1; default 0.4
  - `duration_132` Duration in seconds — 2…15, step 1; default 5
  - `ref_image_size_136` Reference detail — match is faster, max holds identity better (several times slower) — one of: match, max; default match
  - `steps_124` Steps (8 is what this checkpoint was distilled for) — 4…16, step 1; default 8

### `video_fastvideo_fasth3_i2v`

**Start or end on your picture** · model: **FastVideo FastH3 — video with sound, from a first and/or last frame (8 steps)** · makes **video**

Give a first picture, a last picture, or both, and describe what happens: the video starts there, lands there, or travels between them, with sound. Use it to make a clip finish exactly on a poster or a frame you designed.

> Write a scene and get a short film back with its own soundtrack — and optionally pin how it starts, how it ends, or both. Give a FIRST frame and the clip begins there. Give a LAST frame and it arrives there. Give both and the model travels between them, which is the way to animate between two stills. Give neither and it is plain text-to-video. A slot you leave empty is removed from the graph, so it cannot influence the result. ★ Pick the shape that matches your first frame. The model stretches the first frame to fill the video, so a portrait picture in a widescreen video comes out squashed. The LAST frame is treated differently — it is cropped to fit rather than stretched, so its shape matters less. Write the prompt the way this model expects: bind each picture to its moment in the clip first, then describe the shot. Pictures are numbered in the order they are given, so the first frame is <Picture 1>, and the last frame is <Picture 2> when there is a first frame but <Picture 1> when it is alone. • First frame only (the default prompt): "For the target video, at 0.00 seconds into the target video, <Picture 1> (from [Shot 1]) is fully referenced." • Last frame only: "How the reference pictures align with the target video — <Picture 1> (from [Shot 1]) aligns with the 5.17-second mark of the target video." • Both: "How the reference pictures align with the target video — <Picture 1> (from [Shot 1]) aligns with the 0.00-second mark of the target video; <Picture 2> (from [Shot 1]) aligns with the 5.17-second mark of the target video." The end mark is the clip's real length: the duration is rounded up to the model's frame grid, so 5 seconds gives 124 frames, which is 5.17 s (124 ÷ 24). Then write "integrated_multimodal_description: [Shot 1] …". Then describe camera, action and sound in that one block. Naming the audio ("we hear rain on metal, a distant siren") is what earns a deliberate soundtrack rather than an invented one. With no frames at all you can drop the binding line and write the description alone. This is MiniMax H3 distilled by FastVideo to 8 sampling steps, so it is several times quicker than the full model. This checkpoint was not distilled for reference pictures. For several reference pictures, use the "Put your pictures in a video" card (FastH3 OmniRef, also 8 steps) or the slower, more polished Pika H3 Flex card "Make a polished film from pictures".

Prompting: [MiniMax H3 — official video prompt guide](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3/blob/main/docs/VIDEO_PROMPT_WRITING_GUIDE_base_en.md) · [FastVideo FastH3 8-Step V2 — the distilled checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/FastVideo/FastVideo-FastH3-8-Step-V2)
Tip: Bind each picture to its time first (a first frame at 0.00 s, a last frame at the clip's end: 5.17 s for 5 s), then write one block covering framing, camera move, action and the sound.

Columns: `prompt` (Prompt — bind each picture to its time (first frame 0.00 s, last frame the clip's end), then the shot, action and sound) · `seed` · `image` First frame — optional (the clip starts here) (image, optional) · `image2` Last frame — optional (the clip ends here) (image, optional)

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):
  - `resolutionselector_aspect_ratio_143` Shape of the video — match your first frame, it is stretched to fit — one of: 1:1 (Square), 2:3 (Portrait Photo), 3:2 (Photo), 3:4 (Portrait Standard), 4:3 (Standard), 9:16 (Portrait Widescreen), 16:9 (Widescreen), 21:9 (Ultrawide); default 16:9 (Widescreen)
  - `resolutionselector_megapixels_143` Size in megapixels (at 16:9: 0.4 ≈ 864×480, 1.0 ≈ 1376×768) — 0.2…1, step 0.1; default 0.4
  - `primitivefloat_value_105_111` Duration in seconds — 1…12, step 1; default 5
  - `basicscheduler_steps_105_9` Steps (8 is what this checkpoint was distilled for) — 4…16, step 1; default 8

### `video_ltx2_3_ic_lora_ingredients`

**Turn a reference sheet into video** · model: **LTX 2.3 IC-LoRA — reference sheet to video (ingredients + audio)** · makes **video**

Upload one sheet showing your character, a prop and a place as panels tiled edge to edge (no wide black margins, no text), then describe a scene; the video keeps all three looking just like the sheet, with sound. Pick it to keep a character consistent from shot to shot.

> Generate a new video whose characters, props and location match a reference sheet, made by hand or with the "Place characters with boxes" card (MOSS base), as in this card's example. A page from Dynamic Charactersheet krea2 is only a starting point: remove its titles and labels (the sheet must carry no text) and add a panel of the location, which it does not draw. Upload ONE composite image with no text, a clean panel for each element — a face close-up and full-body turnaround for each character, a product-style view of each prop, and one wide shot of the location — and the panels TILED EDGE TO EDGE so they fill the sheet, separated by thin black lines (like ComfyUI's own example sheet). Then describe what happens. LTX 2.3 with the Ingredients IC-LoRA keeps those elements consistent through the clip and generates matching audio (dialogue written in quotes is spoken). Write the prompt in two parts, the way the model was trained: first describe the panels on the sheet ("Reference sheet: …"), then the shot, action and sound ("Generated video: …"). Bigger panels carry over better, and anything that isn't on the sheet won't stay consistent. Duration must be at least 5 seconds (the model needs 121+ frames). The model was trained at 768×448; the default size looks sharper but takes longer (1280×720 asked; LTX rounds the height down to a multiple of 32, so the video comes out 1280×704), and the sheet is letterboxed with black to fit. "Reference strength" controls how strongly the sheet is followed; it starts at 1.4, the model card's own setting. ★ The layout of the sheet matters more than any setting. Measured on this machine: a sheet of small panels floating in wide black margins came back as ITSELF — the panels laid out on black with invented lettering — at strength 1.0, 1.4 and 1.8, and even on the full LTX 2.3 dev model; the same card with ComfyUI's example sheet, and with the same clockmaker redrawn edge to edge, filmed the scene. A sheet can still show through (a small copy of a panel in the room), so try another seed if one does.

Prompting: [LTX-2.3 prompt guide — Lightricks blog](https://ltx.io/blog/ltx-2-3-prompt-guide) · [LTX prompting guide](https://docs.ltx.io/open-source-model/usage-guides/prompting-guide)
Tip: Longer, detailed prompts beat short ones: describe the action and camera over time in one present-tense paragraph, and match the prompt length to the clip length.

Columns: `prompt` (Prompt (describe the sheet, then the shot / action / dialogue)) · `seed` · `image` Reference sheet (character / prop / location panels tiled edge to edge, no text) (image, required)

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):
  - `primitiveint_value_715` Duration (seconds — 5 minimum) — 5…10, step 1; default 5
  - `resizeandpadimage_target_width_722` Width — 256…1920, step 16; default 1280
  - `resizeandpadimage_target_height_722` Height — 256…1920, step 16; default 720
  - `loraloadermodelonly_strength_model_129_195` Reference strength (how closely the sheet is followed) — 0…2, step 0.05; default 1.4

### `image_p_h3_image_edit`

**Change a picture by asking** · model: **P-H3-Image — edit a picture** · makes **image** · experimental

Upload a picture and say what to change: "make it night", "paint the door red". Say what must stay as it is, too: its prompt writer, which would do that for you, does not run on this machine yet.

> Pruna's P-H3-Image edits a picture from a request, run here as a LoRA on MiniMax H3. The model edits best from a brief that names what to change and what to keep ("Make it night; keep the people, the building and the framing"); a bare request can make it redraw the whole scene. It comes with a prompt upsampler (a Qwen3.5-9B writer) that looks at the picture and writes that brief. It is off by default and adds about a minute and a half when switched on. The result has the size of the picture you upload (up to 2048 × 2048). It takes 8 steps, without a negative prompt.

Prompting: [P-H3-Image — prompting (Pruna)](https://huggingface.co/PrunaAI/P-H3-Image#prompting)
Tip: A one-line request is enough: the prompt upsampler writes the full prompt. Put any words to be written in quotes.

Columns: `prompt` (What to change — say what to keep, too) · `seed` · `image` Picture to edit (image, required)

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):
  - `upsampler_23` Write an edit brief from my request (prompt upsampler; adds about a minute and a half) — yes / no; default false

**Change or remove things by asking** · model: **Wan 2.2 Bernini-R — AI image editing** · makes **image**

> Edit an image by describing the change in words. Upload an image and type an instruction (e.g. "make it night", "add snow", "turn the car red") — the Bernini-R model (Wan 2.2) regenerates the image following your prompt while keeping the composition. • **Edit type** steers the model — "Image Editing" for normal edits; "Default" is a more neutral prompt. • **Fast mode** (Turbo LoRA) is on by default — ~6 steps, quick and light. Turn it off for slower, higher-quality 40-step runs. For editing guided by a second (reference) image, use the "with reference" version instead.

Prompting: [Bernini — official example edits](https://github.com/bytedance/Bernini/tree/main/assets/testcases)
Tip: One clear instruction: say what changes and what must stay the same. The result keeps your picture's shape (longer side 1280 px).

### `image_qwen_image_2_1_image_edit`

**Edit a photo using reference pictures** · model: **Qwen Image 2.1 — image edit with references** · makes **image**

Upload the photo to change plus up to nine more pictures of things to bring in (an object, a garment, a face) — ten in all is what Qwen documents, though the form has room for sixteen — and write what goes where; you can even draw coloured circles on the photo and name them in the prompt. Qwen documents up to 10; the form offers 16 because that is the node's maximum, and more than 10 is untested. Image 1 is the one being edited; the rest are references the model can borrow from — a garment, a face, a style, a background. Upload Image 1 and those two fields are ignored: the result keeps Image 1's size, because any other size shifts the edit. Say what should STAY as well as what should change — "keep the pose, the face and the background, replace only the jacket" — vague instructions let the model redraw more than you wanted. ### `image_edit_krea2_dynamic_character_sheet`

**Make a full character design sheet** · model: **Krea 2 Turbo — dynamic character sheet (auto-prompt)** · makes **image**

Upload one picture of a character, creature or object and get a whole design page: big hero view, front/side/back, action poses, silhouettes, expressions and close-up details. Nothing to type; the name and labels are invented and may be misspelled.

> Upload one picture of a subject — a person, an anime or game character, an animal, a creature, a robot, a vehicle or an object — and get back a full production-style character sheet on a 3:2 landscape page (1536x1024): a name and short visual description, a big hero view, a front/side/back turnaround, three action poses, silhouettes, an expression (or function) study and six close-up detail crops, all keeping the design from your picture. There is nothing to type. A built-in vision-language model (Qwen3-VL) first looks at your image and writes the long, structured instruction the Dynamic Character Sheet LoRA expects — what kind of subject it is, its signature details, its rendering style — then Krea 2 Turbo draws the sheet. That writing step is why this takes longer than a plain edit. 'Likeness strength' controls how hard the model copies your picture (1 is normal, 3–4 is closer). 'Steps': around 8 sticks more strictly to the layout, 12 adds detail. The names and labels on the sheet are drawn by the image model, so expect the occasional misspelling.

Columns: `seed` · `image` Subject image (a character, person, animal, creature, robot, vehicle or object) (image, required)

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):
  - `krea2editmodelpatch_ref_boost_120` Likeness strength (1 = normal, 3–4 = copy the design more closely) — 0…10, step 0.1; default 1
  - `ksampler_steps_53` Steps (8 = follows the layout more strictly, 12 = more detail) — 6…16, step 1; default 10

### `image_edit_qwen_2_1_relight_composite`

**Relight a pasted object to fit** · model: **Qwen Image 2.1 — relight a composite (blend an object into a background)** · makes **image**

Paste an object onto a background — roughly, white edges and all — and it re-lights the object to match the scene: shade, highlights and a shadow on the ground, so it stops looking stuck on. Use one picture at about 1 megapixel.

> Harmonise the lighting of a composite. Qwen-Image-2.1 with a community relighting adapter (光影溶图, "light-and-shadow blending"): give it a picture where an object has been dropped onto a background and it re-lights the object to match the scene — key light, specular highlights, front-to-back depth, and the contact shadow that makes something look like it is standing there rather than pasted on. TWO WAYS TO USE IT, both tested on this rig: 1. ONE picture — put your flat composite in Image 1 and leave the rest empty. This is what the adapter was trained for and it needs no special prompt. 2. TWO pictures — put the BACKGROUND in Image 1 and the object in Image 2, and name them in the prompt: "place the character from <image2> into the scene of <image1>, standing on the path…". ⚠ Both halves of that matter. Put the object in Image 1 and you get the object back on its own white background, because the result always follows Image 1 — and a prompt that never says <image1>/<image2> gives the model nothing to connect. ⚠ In this mode the model decides how big the object is: in one run here a lantern came out as tall as the cottage behind it. When size matters, paste the object yourself at the right size and use the one-picture way above. ★ The graph puts the trigger word 'pengyu' in front of the prompt: without it the adapter is effectively inert. The default is the author's own recommended wording, kept verbatim (including its Chinese punctuation) because that is the phrasing it was trained alongside. Add where the light comes from if it picks the wrong direction. ★ Set 'Relight strength' to 0 for the base model on the same seed with everything else identical — that one field is the whole comparison. Measured here on a cartoon figure pasted onto a dark castle: with the adapter the figure is pulled down to the scene's gloomy key light and the white cut-out fringe at its feet disappears; without it the figure stays brightly lit and still reads as pasted on. ⚠ Trained at about 1 megapixel, so stay near 1 MP. It re-renders rather than compositing pixel-for-pixel, so fine print, faces and logos can change — check them. Licence: the adapter is published by RunningHub on behalf of its author with no explicit licence, and the Qwen-Image-2.1 base it runs on is Qwen Research — research and evaluation, not commercial work.

Prompting: [The adapter’s own model card (trigger word + recommended prompt)](https://huggingface.co/RunningHubAI/rh-qwen-image-2.1-lora-2104918997757157378) · [Qwen-Image-2.1 — official model card](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1)
Tip: 'pengyu' is added for you. With one composite the default wording is enough; with a separate object and background you must name them as <image1> and <image2>, and the background goes in Image 1.

Columns: `seed` · `image` Image 1 — your flat composite, OR (for two pictures) the BACKGROUND. ⚠ The result always follows this picture, so the background belongs here, never the object (<image1>) (image, optional) · `image2` Image 2 — the object to place into that background. ⚠ Only used if your prompt names it: “place the object from <image2> into the scene of <image1>…”. Leave empty for a one-picture composite (image, optional) · `image3` Image 3 — optional extra reference, e.g. a picture whose lighting to match (<image3>) (image, optional)

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):
  - `textencodeqwenimage21_prompt_474` What to relight (the trigger word 'pengyu' is added for you); default Apply consistent lighting to the product or object, enhance…
  - `loraloadermodelonly_strength_model_900` Relight strength (0 = the base model alone, for comparison) — 0…1.5, step 0.05; default 1
  - `resolutionselector_aspect_ratio_13` Aspect ratio — only used when you upload NO picture (with Image 1 the result follows it) — one of: 1:1 (Square), 2:3 (Portrait Photo), 3:2 (Photo), 3:4 (Portrait Standard), 4:3 (Standard), 9:16 (Portrait Widescreen), 16:9 (Widescreen), 21:9 (Ultrawide); default 1:1 (Square)
  - `resolutionselector_megapixels_13` Size in megapixels — the adapter was trained at 1, so stay near it — 0.25…2, step 0.25; default 1
  - `ksampler_steps_458` Steps (25 is quick, 40–50 is Qwen’s own setting) — 10…60, step 1; default 25

### `image_edit_qwen_2511_multiple_angles`

**See your subject from another angle** · model: **Qwen Image-Edit 2511 - reshoot from another angle (place the camera)** · makes **image**

Upload one photo of an object or character and place the camera around it — behind, above, closer — and you get the same subject seen from there in a few seconds. The hidden side is invented, so keep the seed fixed to build a matching set.

> Upload one photo and reshoot the same subject from somewhere else: walk the camera round it, raise or lower it, and come in closer. PLACE THE CAMERA, don't describe it. Drag the stage to orbit, scroll to zoom, or use the three sliders. The subject stays put and the camera moves, so what you see in the little scene is where the shot is taken from. WHAT THE MODEL ACTUALLY RECEIVES is the line of chips under the stage - something like 'right side view / elevated shot / medium shot'. That is the whole instruction, and it is worth understanding because the control is coarser than it looks: there are 8 positions around the subject, 4 heights and 3 framings - 96 shots in all. Nudging the slider a few degrees usually changes nothing, and the chips are what tell you when it does. Move until a chip changes. FAST MODE (on by default) runs the 4-step Lightning adapter: a few seconds a shot, which is what makes it practical to try a dozen angles. Turning it off runs the slow 40-step path, about 2½ minutes a shot; on a test shot here it looked no better. WHAT TO EXPECT: it invents the side of the subject it has never seen, so a back view is a plausible back rather than the truth. Keep the seed fixed while you move the camera and the invented details stay consistent from shot to shot, which is what makes a usable turnaround. The result comes back at about 1 megapixel whatever you upload. Licence: the Qwen-Image-Edit base is Qwen Research - research and evaluation, not commercial work.

Prompting: [The adapter's own model card (fal) - what it was trained to do](https://huggingface.co/fal/Qwen-Image-Edit-2511-Multiple-Angles-LoRA)
Tip: There is nothing to write: placing the camera IS the prompt. The chips under the stage are the exact words the model receives.

Columns: `seed` · `image` The subject to reshoot - one clear photo (image, required)

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):
  - `cameraangle_221` Where the camera stands; default {"horizontal": 180, "vertical": 0, "zoom": 5}
  - `primitiveboolean_value_219_168` Fast mode (4-step adapter - seconds instead of over two minutes) — yes / no; default true
  - `loraloadermodelonly_strength_model_219_220` Adapter strength (lower it if the subject drifts) — 0…1.5, step 0.05; default 1

## Preparing a picture (depth, edges, masks) (`preprocessor`, 6)

### `utility_ltx2_5_video_deblur_upscale`

**Enlarge a video 2×, adding detail** · model: **LTX 2.5 — 2× generative video upscale (keeps original audio)** · makes **video**

Upload a small video that has sound; it redraws it at up to twice the size with new fine detail, keeping the original sound. Pick it to finish a quick draft — it invents detail, so it is not for exact restoration.

> Enlarge a small video up to 2× with new, sharp detail. Upload a clip and LTX 2.5 re-renders every frame with Lightricks' Pixel Spatial Upscaler IC-LoRA (a generative 2× upscaler — it invents detail, it is not a deblur or restoration model), keeping the original motion and the original soundtrack (the sound is passed through the model's audio decoder, not regenerated, and the last fraction of a second — sound included — can be trimmed to fit LTX's frame grid). For heavy blur or compression damage, the SeedVR2 video cards are the faithful choice. Your clip must have a sound track — silent videos fail. "Output size" is the short side of the result (576 ≈ 1024×576 for a 16:9 clip). The model reads your video at half that size and rebuilds the detail, so raise it to 704 or 1088 for a bigger, sharper result — it gets slower. The prompt is optional: a short description of what's in the clip, or just the look you want, can help. You can also tick "Use a start image" and upload a sharp still of the first frame to anchor the result to it; leave it unticked to skip it. Only the start of your clip is used ("Clip length used", default 5 s). This is a fast single 8-step pass.

Prompting: [LTX IC-LoRA guide — Lightricks](https://docs.ltx.io/open-source-model/usage-guides/ic-lo-ra) · [LTX prompting guide](https://docs.ltx.io/open-source-model/usage-guides/prompting-guide)
Tip: The prompt is optional: a short description of what's in the clip is enough — your video does the work.

Columns: `prompt` (Prompt (optional — what's in the clip / the look you want)) · `seed` · `image` Start image, optional (a sharp still of the first frame) (image, optional) · `video` Video to enlarge (must have a sound track) (video, required)

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):
  - `resizeimagemasknode_resize_type_shorter_size_5548_5026` Output size (short side, in pixels — snapped to a multiple of 64) — 256…1088, step 64; default 576
  - `video_slice_duration_9900` Clip length used (seconds, max 10 — only the start of your video is processed) — 1…10, step 0.5; default 5

### `utility_relayvsr_video_x2_upscale`

**Enlarge a video twice, in one pass** · model: **RelayVSR — video upscale 2x** · makes **video** · experimental

Give it a video clip and get it back twice as wide and twice as tall, sharper, in one fast pass; the sound and the frame rate are kept.

> Upscale a video exactly 2x with RelayVSR, built into ComfyUI since 0.45. A large Wan-based model paints reference latents for keyframes (one every 15 frames) in one sampling step, and a light "Flash" decoder carries them across every frame, so a clip is restored in one streaming pass. This is the 2x pair retrained by LightX2V for the step after H3 generation; the factor comes from the weights, not from a setting. On a 4-second 864x480 clip made by the H3 turbo card it returned 1728x960 in about 18 seconds, all 96 frames at 24 fps with the sound, using about 5 GB of graphics memory: denim seams, hair and the faces in the background came out clearly sharper than a plain enlargement. Only the part of the clip between "Start at" and "Length" is upscaled (5 seconds at most), so a long upload cannot exhaust the card. "Detail kept" sets how much of the detail the decoder adds over a plain bicubic enlargement is kept (1 = all of it). Square videos work since the comfy-kitchen fix of 2026-11-12 (Maintenance: Re-apply the comfy-kitchen fixes); before it they failed on this rig. Crop it to 16:9 or 9:16 first. Experimental.

Columns: `seed` · `video` Video to enlarge (video, required)

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):
  - `start_202` Start at (seconds) — 0…3600, step 0.1; default 0
  - `length_202` Length to enlarge (seconds) — 1…5, step 0.5; default 5
  - `detail_108_104` Detail kept (1 = all the detail the model adds) — 0…1, step 0.05; default 1

### `utility_video_segment_sam3`

**Isolate a named object in video** · model: **SAM3 — text-prompted video segmentation** · makes **video**

Give it a video and type the name of something in it; you get a black-and-white video where only that thing is white, ready for cutting out in editing. Write 'person:5' to catch up to five of them.

Upload a video and type what to track (e.g. "person", "dog", "red car") — SAM3 finds that object in every frame and outputs a black-and-white **mask video** (white = the object, black = everything else), ready to use as a matte / luma key in compositing. Tip: use a short, concrete noun or noun phrase. Lower the detection threshold to catch more (looser), raise it to be stricter. Output frames line up 1:1 with the source.

Columns: `video` Source video (video, required)

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):

  - `threshold_114_101` Detection threshold — 0.1…0.9, step 0.05; default 0.5

### `utility_video_frame_interpolation`

**Make a video smoother or slow-motion** · model: **Frame interpolation (FILM) — smoother or slow-motion video** · makes **video**

Give it a video and get it back with new in-between frames: smoother at the same speed, or turned into slow motion. Works best on fast movement.

> Make a video smoother — or turn it into slow motion. FILM generates in-between frames, multiplying the frame count by your chosen factor (2× = twice as many frames). • **Keep real-time speed** checked → the clip plays at the same speed but looks smoother (higher frame rate). • Unchecked → the extra frames stretch the clip into **slow motion** at the original frame rate. The original audio is carried through — best with 'keep real-time speed' on; in slow-motion mode the audio won't match the longer video.

Columns: `video` Source video (video, required)

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):
  - `multiplier_16_9` Frame multiplier (×) — 2…8, step 1; default 2
  - `keep_realtime_speed_16_13` Keep real-time speed (uncheck for slow-motion) — yes / no; default true

### `utility_seedvr2_hd_upscale`

**Restore a video to 1080p** · model: **SeedVR2 — video upscale to HD (1080p)** · makes **video**

Give it a short, soft or low-quality video and get it back at 1080p, cleaned of blur and compression blocks with edges sharpened — texture lost completely is not invented back; the sound and frame rate are kept.

> Upscale and restore a video to HD with SeedVR2, a diffusion-based super-resolution model that restores detail frame-by-frame with temporal consistency. Upload a clip and it's re-rendered at the target resolution, keeping the original frame rate and audio. It is a faithful restorer: on a damaged test clip it removed every compression block and sharpened edges and hair, but a sweater knit the copy had lost entirely did not come back. Very heavy — processing every frame at HD takes a while, so keep clips short. Change the seed to re-roll the generated detail.

Columns: `seed` · `video` Source video (video, required)

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):
  - `resolution_10` Target resolution (px, SHORTEST edge) — 480…2160, step 8; default 1080

### `utility_seedvr2_3b_int8_video_upscale`

**Restore and enlarge a video ×2** · model: **SeedVR2 3B (int8) — video upscale & restore** · makes **video**

Give it a short video and get it back up to twice as wide and tall, with compression blocks and blur cleaned up and edges sharpened — texture the copy lost completely is not invented back. It can trim the clip first and match the original colours.

> Upload a video and SeedVR2 rebuilds every frame at a larger size, restoring real detail (textures, edges, blocky compression) instead of just stretching the pixels. The original frame rate and audio are kept. It is a faithful restorer: on a damaged test clip it removed every compression block and sharpened edges and hair, but a sweater knit the copy had lost entirely did not come back. This is the light int8 build of the 3B model, running on ComfyUI's built-in SeedVR2 support. Upscale factor multiplies the size of your clip, up to ×2: 540p becomes 1080p, and 1080p becomes 4K, which is already very heavy. Time grows with the output size times the number of frames, so keep clips short and the factor modest. Turn on Trim to process just a few seconds (start time + length), and turn on "Process in chunks" if a longer clip fails for lack of memory. If the colours drift away from the original, pick a colour correction ("lab" is the most faithful). Change the seed to re-roll the generated detail. The time estimate shown is from the last calibration; longer or larger clips take proportionally longer.

Columns: `seed` · `video` Source video (video, required)

Settings (a column named by the key; empty keeps the default):
  - `resizeimagemasknode_resize_type_multiplier_66_57` Upscale factor (×2 = twice as wide and tall — the maximum) — 1…2, step 0.5; default 2
  - `comfyswitchnode_switch_66_81` Trim the clip before upscaling — yes / no; default false
  - `video_slice_start_time_66_79` Trim start (seconds) — 0…3600, step 0.1; default 0
  - `video_slice_duration_66_79` Trim length (seconds, 0 = to the end) — 0…600, step 0.1; default 5
  - `primitiveboolean_value_66_105` Process in chunks (for long clips / out-of-memory errors) — yes / no; default false
  - `seedvr2postprocessing_color_correction_method_66_59` Colour correction (match the original colours) — one of: lab, wavelet, adain, none; default none
